title: Vesper and the Garden
premise: Tamsin Halloran has spent their whole life in the valley of Vesper, where the dead whisper through bone and magic cannot cross the ridge line. When a dying courier presses a map into their hands, Tamsin learns the valley's safety is a cage built by a king who bound his own soul to something ancient wearing his crown. Guided by the map, a disgraced hedge-witch, and a soldier who deserted the crown, Tamsin must reach the capital before the thirteenth moon turns and the binding becomes permanent. In the end, Tamsin chooses to unbind the king at terrible cost—losing their ability to hear the dead—and returns to Vesper not as an invisible survivor, but as the founder of a found family that no longer needs hiding.
about_author: Wren Reyes is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing funeral customs across three continents before turning to fiction. They write about grief, stubborn hope, and the people history forgets to name.

chapters.title: The Valley That Forgets
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. We meet them carving memorial bones in Vesper, hearing the dead murmur through their work while the valley's anti-magic ward hums at the ridgeline. A routine commission reveals a grave that shouldn't exist—one holding a body only days old, though no one has entered the valley in years. Beat: quiet unease beneath domestic calm.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Ford
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The stranger from the impossible grave stumbles into Tamsin's workshop, half-dead, clutching a leather map case. He speaks of a king, a thirteenth moon, and 'the thing that answers when he prays.' He dies pressing the map into Tamsin's hands. Beat: fear and reluctant responsibility.

chapters.title: What the Bones Said
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The dead stranger's voice lingers in the bone Tamsin carves from his remains, repeating fragments: coordinates, a warning, a name—Maren. The valley elders demand the map be surrendered; Tamsin lies for the first time in their life. Beat: first act of defiance.

chapters.title: Maren of the Ash Road
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Introduce Maren, a hedge-witch exiled from the capital, living rough beyond the ridge. She recognizes the map's sigils as royal binding-work and realizes the courier reached Vesper deliberately—the valley was the one place the crown couldn't track it. Beat: dread sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: Crossing the Ridge
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin slips past the ward line at night, and for the first time feels magic touch the world—overwhelming, loud, alive. Their bone-hearing changes: outside the valley, they hear the dead everywhere, a roar instead of a whisper. Beat: awe curdling into terror.

chapters.title: The Hedge-Witch's Bargain
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Tamsin finds Maren; neither trusts the other. Maren agrees to guide Tamsin to the capital if Tamsin uses their hearing to find her sister, taken by the crown's tithe of magicians years ago. Beat: wary alliance forged from mutual need.

chapters.title: Ashes on the Pilgrim Road
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. On the road, they pass villages emptied by the king's conscription, and Tamsin hears the recent dead begging for names. They begin carving bones for strangers, unable to stop themselves. Beat: compassion as burden; the cost of listening.

chapters.title: The Deserter
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram Vey, a soldier who fled the Royal Guard after refusing an order, shadows the pair, convinced they're crown agents. Confrontation turns to uneasy truce when Tamsin relays a message from Bram's dead commander—an apology he never expected to hear. Beat: guilt met with grace.

chapters.title: Thirteen Moons
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. At a waystation, Maren deciphers more of the map: the binding completes on the thirteenth turn of the moon, twelve nights away. After that, the thing wearing the crown will no longer need the king's body at all. Beat: the clock starts ticking in earnest.

chapters.title: The Tithe House
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. They infiltrate a tithe house where captured magicians are drained for the crown's use. Tamsin finds Maren's sister Sefa alive but hollowed, her magic harvested. Rescue succeeds partially; Sefa cannot speak but grips Maren's hand. Beat: rage and grief braided together.

chapters.title: What Wears the Crown
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram reveals what he saw in the palace: the king alone in the prayer chapel, talking to something in the walls, his shadow moving wrong. The entity is an old god of hunger, bound into the royal line generations ago—and it has been eating its way outward ever since. Beat: the true scale of the threat revealed.

chapters.title: The City of Bells
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The trio reaches the capital, deafening with dead voices. Tamsin nearly drowns in the noise until Sefa, wordless, teaches them to shape the sound into something bearable—a found-family moment amid horror. Beat: connection as survival skill.

chapters.title: An Audience Refused
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Attempts to warn the court fail; the queen regent is either complicit or enchanted. Maren is recognized and nearly arrested; Bram burns his old oath publicly to cover their escape. Beat: the system itself is the enemy; no rescue from above.

chapters.title: The Chapel Below
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Following the map's final markings, they find the under-chapel where the original binding was made—carved bones, centuries old, singing with the trapped god's hunger. Tamsin realizes the binding can be undone only from inside, by someone who can hear it. Beat: the trap closes around the plan.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Bell Tower
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. A former comrade captures Bram and offers him reinstatement in exchange for the others. Bram plays along long enough to learn the crown knows everything—then warns Tamsin at cost of his own capture. Beat: loyalty proven through sacrifice.

chapters.title: The King Who Prays
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Through a smuggled audience, Tamsin meets King Aldous: a hollowed man who begs them, in a lucid moment, to end it. He gives them the last piece of the rite—his own consent, spoken aloud. Beat: pity for the monster's hostage; moral complexity deepens.

chapters.title: Twelfth Night
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. The group prepares the unbinding with stolen tithe-house magicians, including a flickering-recovered Sefa. The plan requires someone to stand inside the binding circle and hold the line open while the god is cut loose. Everyone volunteers; Tamsin quietly decides it must be them. Beat: dread and resolve.

chapters.title: The Thirteenth Turn
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Climax. Under the full thirteenth moon, the rite begins. The god offers Tamsin everything—their dead, their valley, their lost years—in exchange for walking away. Tamsin refuses, holds the circle as the king's soul is cut free, and the backlash takes their bone-hearing forever. Beat: sacrifice at the peak of the arc.

chapters.title: Aftermath of a Hollow Crown
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The god, unbound and starving without an anchor, dissipates over the city like frost in sun. The king dies human at last; Bram, freed, chooses to help build a regency council rather than seize power. Beat: power refused is power redeemed.

chapters.title: Silence
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Grieving the loss of the voices that defined them, Tamsin carves one final bone—their own memorial to the dead they can no longer hear. Maren, Sefa, and Bram sit with them through the night. Beat: mourning transformed by companionship.

chapters.title: The Road Back to Vesper
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. The four travel home together, gathering strays along the way—freed tithed magicians with nowhere to go. The valley elders resist, but the ward, weakened by the god's fall, can no longer keep the world out—or the family in. Beat: home redefined as people, not walls.

chapters.title: Vesper and the Garden
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Epilogue. A season later, the workshop has become a school: bone-carving taught openly, the dead honored rather than feared. Tamsin plants a garden over the stranger's grave and, in the silence where voices used to be, finds something quieter and harder—peace. Beat: resolution; survival's price paid, and worth it.
